title: I Choose You
hookLine: Lakshmi choosing Vishnu from the ocean of milk, and the line where the hymn stops saying 'her' and says 'you'
carry: prapatti: taking refuge is a choice
tomorrow: why is the fortune goddess's tree so hard to crack?

lines: A PERSON TALKING TO A PERSON.
cards: A cover letter begins: to whom it may concern. Polite, careful, written to a title. Three paragraphs later, if the job matters enough, it starts to sound like a person talking to a person.
A speech at a retirement party can go the same way: it starts about the colleague, and ends turned toward her, glass up, speaking to her directly. Something like that happens in the Sri Sukta today.
For several lines the singer has talked about the goddess. Called her near. Described her.
Then, at the end of one line, the pronoun changes.

teach.b: A story first. The Bhagavata Purana tells that when Lakshmi rose from the churned ocean, she looked over the gods, sages and demons, found a flaw in each, and chose Vishnu, placing her garland on him. She chose.
Today the Sri Sukta turns that around. Here's the line, in paraphrase.
Bright as the moon, blazing with glory, Sri, cherished by the gods, generous: I take refuge in her, the lotus one.
May misfortune be gone from me. I choose you. The first half is still the portrait.
Then a step closer. I take refuge in her. Refuge is what you look for when you've run out of ways to manage on your own.
The singer isn't only admiring her now; he's placing himself under her shelter. Then the request: may misfortune be gone. The word is Alakshmi, and she'll come back with a face of her own.
And then the last two words. Tvam vrine. I choose you.
All along it's been she, her, Sri. Suddenly it's you. The singer turns and speaks to her face to face.
She chose once; now he chooses her. Here is the teaching.
His words for refuge, sharanam prapadye, gave Hindus a name for a whole path: prapatti, surrender, taking refuge in God.

In the Sri Vaishnava tradition of South India, devotees take refuge in Vishnu through Sri, honored as the mother who brings them in. Surrender, in this tradition, isn't giving up. It's choosing whom to turn to.

how: Some Hindus recite the Sri Sukta in full during Lakshmi worship at home or in temples, so this verse of refuge is spoken as part of the whole hymn.

o: a hymn that curses the bad luck of an enemy
a hymn whose singer turns and chooses Sri herself
a contract trading worship for a fixed reward

s: the singer only ever speaks about the goddess, never to her
at the end of this line he turns and says: I choose you.
the line asks for misfortune to be gone
may Alakshmi, misfortune, be gone from me.
prapatti, the Hindu path of taking refuge, comes from the same words the singer uses
sharanam prapadye, I take refuge: Sri Vaishnavas call their path of surrender prapatti.

games.q: you've been describing the goddess line after line, always as 'her'. now you're in trouble and need shelter. what do you do?
o: keep describing her, politely, from a distance.
turn and speak to her: I choose you.
ask the fire to carry the message for you.
games.why: the singer takes refuge in her, asks for misfortune to go, and then turns: tvam vrine, I choose you. the pronoun changes from her to you.

practice: Bring to mind something that's been weighing on you, a stretch of bad luck or a worry you keep circling, and let it be there. Then turn toward your shelter the way the hymn turns from her to you.

If you pray, you can say the old words of refuge in your own language, 'I take refuge in you,' to the goddess, or to God, and rest there; if you don't, ask yourself gently where you go for shelter, a person, a place, a practice, and rest under it.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Sukta. The hymn where the singer takes refuge in Sri, asks for misfortune to go, and turns to say: I choose you.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tvāṃ vṛṇe, 'I choose you,' the last words of this line of the Sri Sukta.

carryVoice: Your line: prapatti, taking refuge is a choice. From she to you: the singer chooses where to turn. Same time tomorrow.
